note: Propagation reference for Cuttings Garden. Facts curated from common horticulture references. Any entry we are not fully confident about carries "verify": true so it can be checked before the demo. Toxicity lives in the separate toxicity.json (our flagship safety dataset) and is joined by scientificName at load time.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut 0.5-1 cm below a node (the small brown bump where a leaf meets the vine). Every cutting needs at least one node and one leaf.
species.notes: One of the easiest plants to propagate. Aerial-root nubs at the nodes root fastest.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut just below a node that has an aerial root attached, keeping one leaf. Submerge the node and aerial root; keep the leaf dry.
species.notes: Including an aerial root dramatically speeds rooting.

species.cutLocationDescription: Snip 0.5-1 cm below a node, leaving 2-3 leaves per cutting. Remove the lowest leaf so the bare node sits in water.
species.notes: Vining philodendrons root very reliably in a windowsill glass.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a healthy leaf into 8-10 cm sections. Mark which edge faced down: sections only root from the basal (lower) edge.
species.notes: Slow but forgiving. Variegated types lose their stripe from leaf cuttings; divide instead to keep it.

species.cutLocationDescription: Snip a plantlet (spiderette) from its runner. Plantlets that already show root nubs can go straight to soil.
species.notes: Pet-safe and nearly foolproof: a great first propagation.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take 10-15 cm tip cuttings just below a node. Strip leaves from the lower half before placing in water.
species.notes: Vigorous once rooted; can be invasive outdoors, so keep it contained.

species.cutLocationDescription: Pups sprout from the soil beside the mother stem. Cut a pup 1-2 cm below the soil line with a bit of its own stem, then root it.
species.notes: Famous as the shareable 'friendship plant' because it makes so many pups.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take a leaf with 1-2 cm of stem, or a short stem cutting below a node. Let the cut air-dry for an hour, then root.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Compact and slow-growing, ideal for small spaces.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take a cutting with 2-3 nodes and at least one leaf pair. Root the lower node; keep the leaves above the water.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Never cut off the old flower spurs: hoyas rebloom from them.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take a tip cutting with 2-3 leaves below a node, or air-layer the stem. Blot the milky sap and dip in rooting hormone.
species.notes: Sap is a skin irritant; wear gloves. Air-layering has the highest success rate.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take a 25-30 cm stem cutting with 2-3 leaves below a node. Dip in rooting hormone and keep humidity high.
species.notes: Slow and temperamental. Sap is irritating; wear gloves.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a 10 cm piece just below a node. Almost every node will root; strip the lowest leaves.
species.notes: Roots extremely fast, which makes it a satisfying beginner cutting.

species.cutLocationDescription: Pull a whole leaflet with a bit of its base, or divide the underground rhizomes. Leaflets grow a new rhizome first, then roots.
species.notes: Very slow (can take months) but almost impossible to kill.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a healthy leaf with 2-3 cm of stem at a 45-degree angle. Root the stem; a plantlet forms at its base.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Keep water off the fuzzy leaves to avoid spotting.

species.cutLocationDescription: Twist off a Y-shaped piece of 2-3 segments at a joint. Let it callus for a day, then set the base in barely-moist mix.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Do not root in water: the segments rot easily.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take a stem cutting or a clean whole leaf. Let the wound callus 2-3 days, then lay it on dry succulent mix.
species.notes: Do not propagate in water: it rots. Water only after roots appear.

species.cutLocationDescription: Gently twist a whole leaf off the stem so none of it tears. Callus 3 days, lay on dry soil, mist weekly.
species.notes: Pet-safe. A clean, complete leaf base is essential; torn leaves fail.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a 10-15 cm strand. Lay it on top of the soil and press the nodes (where pearls meet the stem) into contact.
species.notes: Roots along the buried nodes. Keep barely moist until established.

species.cutLocationDescription: Separate a pup (offset) that has a few of its own roots from the base of the mother plant. Leaf cuttings rarely root.
species.notes: Let any cut surface callus before potting. Do not root in water.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a 10 cm stem just below a leaf pair (node). Strip the lower leaves, keep the top two pairs, and root in water.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Pinch flowers off to keep it leafy. A grocery-store basil pot is free cuttings.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut just below a node on a healthy runner. Almost any node will root.
species.notes: Roots aggressively. Grow in a pot: in the ground it takes over.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take 10 cm semi-woody tip cuttings. Strip the lower needles and root in water or barely-moist mix.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Overwatering is the main killer of rosemary cuttings.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take 5-8 cm green (non-woody) tip cuttings just below a node. Strip the lower leaves and root.
species.notes: Green tips root far more readily than woody stems. See toxicity note before letting pets near it.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a 10 cm stem below a node, strip the lower leaves, and root in water.
species.notes: Roots easily on a sunny windowsill. See toxicity note before letting pets near it.

species.cutLocationDescription: Take a semi-woody side shoot with a heel. Strip the lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and set in gritty mix.
species.notes: Does not like water propagation. Needs sharp drainage to avoid rot.

species.cutLocationDescription: Keep the bottom 3-4 cm with the root plate intact. Stand it upright in a glass with the roots submerged.
species.notes: Regrows in days from grocery scraps: the flagship food-waste win. Note: toxic to pets (allium).

species.cutLocationDescription: Save the intact base (bottom 5 cm). Sit it in a shallow dish of water; new stalks push up from the centre.
species.notes: Move to soil once roots and a leafy centre appear for full-size regrowth.

species.cutLocationDescription: Keep the intact base (bottom 3-4 cm). Sit it in 1-2 cm of water; a new leafy rosette grows from the centre.
species.notes: Pet-safe. Regrowth is smaller than the original but great for garnishes.

species.cutLocationDescription: Grow from saved seeds: rinse, dry 2 days, then sow 0.5 cm deep in warm seed-starting mix.
species.notes: The ripe fruit is safe, but the foliage is in the nightshade family. See toxicity note; verify before pet claims.

species.cutLocationDescription: Snap off a 'sucker' (the shoot in the V between the main stem and a branch), 10-15 cm long, and root it in water.
species.notes: Clones the parent plant for free. Green foliage and stems are toxic to pets.

species.cutLocationDescription: Cut a piece of rhizome with at least one visible 'eye' (growth bud). Let it dry a day, then plant eye-up just under the soil.
species.notes: Pet-safe. A knob of grocery ginger becomes a whole plant.
